payload.title: The Unfinished Debt

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Many works of fiction follow characters who live in the long shadow of something they once did wrong. A son who failed to protect a sibling may spend decades caring for strangers. A deserter may return home and work his neighbor's fields without pay. A woman who betrayed a friend may confess to everyone except the person she wronged. Atonement can steady a life by giving it a purpose. It can also take over that life, because the effort to repair a wrong can shut out new connections, drive new mistakes, or keep the wrong at the center of who the character is. A work may also ask a harder question: whether the debt can ever be paid at all.

Either from your own reading or from the list below, choose a work of fiction in which a character's attempt to atone for a past wrong shapes the choices that character makes afterward. Then, in a well-written essay, analyze how the character's pursuit of atonement and the question of whether it can be completed contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Do not merely summarize the plot.

Your essay should:
- State a defensible thesis about how the idea in the prompt contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole.
- Support the argument with specific, accurate evidence from the work you chose, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Do not merely summarize the plot.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.

parts.model_answer:
In Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner, Amir spends most of his adult life trying to make up for the winter afternoon when he watched Hassan get raped in an alley and did nothing. The novel never lets him pay that debt back, though. Hassan is dead before Amir even tries, so the only person who could forgive him is gone. What Hosseini suggests instead is that atonement can't be finished; it can only be passed forward, and even then it is partial and has its own costs. Amir does not become "good again" by erasing the wrong. He becomes good by agreeing to carry it.

The first choices Amir makes after the alley are not atonement at all, which matters for how we read the later ones. Amir can't stand to be near Hassan, so he pelts him with pomegranates and begs him to hit back. Hassan just crushes one against his own forehead. Amir wants to be punished because punishment would close the account, and Hassan refuses to do it. Then Amir plants his birthday money and watch under Hassan's mattress so Baba will send him away. Hassan takes the blame, Baba forgives him, and Ali and Hassan leave anyway. In this early section, guilt makes Amir do more harm. He doesn't try to fix the wrong; he tries to get rid of the witness. The pomegranate scene shows that the victim's forgiveness (or his refusal to condemn) is not something Amir can force out of him, and this idea comes back at the end of the book.

When Rahim Khan calls Amir to Pakistan and tells him there is a way to be good again, it looks like the novel is promising completion. But Rahim Khan also reveals that Hassan was Baba's son, so Amir's betrayal was of his own brother. This revelation adds something to the story: guilt runs in the family. Baba built an orphanage and gave to everyone, and Rahim Khan explains these deeds as Baba's way of making up for betraying Ali. Baba's charity helped strangers but never told Hassan the truth. Amir realizes his father's goodness and his father's lie were part of the same thing. So the novel sets up a test: will Amir repeat Baba's pattern of public good deeds covering a private wrong, or will he actually deal with the person his family harmed?

He goes after Sohrab, and the scene with Assef is where Hosseini's symbolism is strongest. Amir gets beaten so badly that he laughs, because for the first time he feels he is getting what he deserved. His lip is split in a way that echoes Hassan's harelip, as if the beating marks him with his brother's face. Then Sohrab saves him with a slingshot, the same weapon Hassan once used to hold Assef off when they were children. This mirroring could be read as Amir's redemption being complete, the past finally reenacted and corrected. I think the details actually point the other way. Amir is still the one being saved, and a child is still doing the brave thing for him. The scene repeats the past, it doesn't reverse it.

The aftermath supports this reading. Amir breaks his promise that Sohrab will never go back to an orphanage, and Sohrab tries to kill himself in the hotel bathtub. Amir's effort to repair one wrong produces a new one, almost exactly like his earlier betrayal of Hassan's trust. Even in America Sohrab barely speaks. The ending, where Amir runs a kite for Sohrab in a park and gets a small lopsided smile, is deliberately small. Amir himself says it doesn't fix everything. The kite brings back the tournament where everything went wrong, but now Amir is the one running for someone else.

So Hosseini does not reward Amir with forgiveness, because the only person who could give it is dead. Instead the novel moves the meaning of atonement from paying off a debt to taking on a duty. Baba's kind of redemption, generous to strangers and silent to the person he wronged, is the version the book rejects. Amir's is incomplete and clumsy, but it is aimed at the right person, and the novel suggests that's as close to good again as anyone gets.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis makes a claim about how the character's pursuit of atonement, and whether it can be completed, contributes to the meaning of the whole work. An example: 'Because the wronged brother is dead, the narrator's charity work can never close the debt, and the novel suggests that guilt must be carried rather than paid off.' Restating the prompt, saying only that a character 'tries to make up for a mistake,' or naming a work without an interpretive claim does not earn the point. The thesis does not need to settle the completion question with a yes or no, but it must take a position on it.

Strong responses identify the specific wrong. They then trace several later choices that the character makes because of it, using concrete references to scenes, actions, dialogue, or images, and explain how each choice develops the claim about atonement. Commentary should consistently link the evidence to the question of completion: does forgiveness arrive, does the victim matter, does the repair become a new harm? Responses that summarize events in order with little explanation of their meaning score 2 at most. Responses with specific, well-chosen evidence and sustained reasoning across the whole essay earn 4.

Sophistication might look like exploring the tension between atonement as healing and atonement as self-punishment or vanity. It might also look like a sharp argument about who has the authority to declare a debt paid, or placing the work's view of atonement within its cultural or historical context, for example inherited or collective guilt. The point must come from argument woven through the essay, not from a single sentence or from elevated vocabulary alone.

- Row A: "What Hosseini suggests instead is that atonement can't be finished; it can only be passed forward, and even then it is partial and has its own costs." - Defensible thesis that takes a clear position on whether atonement can be completed (it can't) and ties it to the meaning of the whole novel. It also sets up a line of reasoning: the victim is gone, so repair has to be passed forward, and repair has costs.
- Row A: "He becomes good by agreeing to carry it." - Makes the thesis sharper by turning the idea of 'being good again' from paying off a debt into carrying a burden, which the closing paragraph comes back to.
- Row B: "Hassan just crushes one against his own forehead." - Specific, accurate scene used as evidence. The commentary that follows explains that Amir wants punishment to 'close the account,' which links the scene to the question of completion.
- Row B: "He doesn't try to fix the wrong; he tries to get rid of the witness." - Commentary reads the framing of Hassan for theft as guilt that causes new harm, which ties directly to the prompt's idea of a mistake driven by guilt.
- Row B: "His lip is split in a way that echoes Hassan's harelip" - Analyzes symbolism and mirroring (the split lip, the slingshot) as literary techniques, so the essay covers more than one technique and how each contributes to meaning, as Row B's top score requires.
- Row B: "Amir's effort to repair one wrong produces a new one" - Follows a later choice driven by repair (the broken orphanage promise) and explains how it makes the repair itself a new harm. The commentary stays tied to the line of reasoning.
- Row C: "This revelation adds something to the story: guilt runs in the family." - Begins a sustained point about inherited guilt. The Baba/Amir comparison runs through the rest of the essay, which gives it a wider context.
- Row C: "This mirroring could be read as Amir's redemption being complete, the past finally reenacted and corrected. I think the details actually point the other way." - Takes on an alternative reading and answers it with evidence from the text, so the complexity isn't oversimplified.
- Row C: "Baba's kind of redemption, generous to strangers and silent to the person he wronged, is the version the book rejects." - Brings the Baba comparison to a conclusion about which kind of atonement the novel approves of. This shows the sophistication is developed across the essay, not stated in a single sentence.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In The Kite Runner, Amir lives for most of his life under the weight of what he did to Hassan, and Hosseini uses his long effort to make up for it to suggest that atonement can never be fully completed, only continued. Amir's attempt to repay the wrong gives his adult life direction, but the novel shows that the person he wronged is gone, so the debt can only be paid in a different form than he first imagined.

The wrong is specific. As a boy in Kabul, Amir hides and watches while Hassan is attacked by Assef in the alley after the kite tournament. Hassan had been loyal to Amir, and Amir did nothing. Afterward Amir makes it worse by driving Hassan and his father Ali out of the house, framing Hassan as a thief. Because Amir's guilt comes from cowardice and betrayal, the repair he later attempts has to be about courage and loyalty.

Amir's later choices are shaped by this. In America he becomes a writer and marries Soraya, but his success feels hollow, because the secret is still there under his life. When Rahim Khan calls him back to Pakistan and says there is a way to be good again, Amir goes, even though it is dangerous. In Afghanistan he learns that Hassan was his half-brother and that Hassan has been killed, leaving a son, Sohrab. Amir's decision to rescue Sohrab from Assef, who now serves the Taliban, is the clearest act of atonement. This time he does not hide. He takes a beating from Assef, and Hosseini makes the violence almost welcome to Amir, as if the pain finally pays for what he allowed before. The split lip he gets is described as a kind of healing, which shows that Amir sees atonement partly as punishment.

However, the novel does not let the repair feel finished. Hassan can never forgive Amir, because Hassan is dead, so the person whose forgiveness matters most is out of reach. Sohrab is also not a simple payment. After the rescue he is traumatized, and when he is threatened with being sent back to an orphanage, he attempts suicide. Amir's good deed does not erase the damage, and it shows that Sohrab is a real person and not just a way for Amir to feel better.

The ending is hopeful but modest. Sohrab barely speaks, and then he gives a small smile when Amir flies a kite for him and offers to run it for him. This moment echoes the kite tournament of the past, and it suggests that Amir has changed. But it is only a smile, not a cure. By making the ending small, Hosseini argues that atonement is not a debt that is paid once but a way of living, a lifelong responsibility to do right by the next generation. Amir is not fully free of his past, yet he is no longer defined only by his failure, and that is the most the novel allows.
- Row A: "Hosseini uses his long effort to make up for it to suggest that atonement can never be fully completed, only continued" - Defensible thesis that takes a position on whether atonement can be completed and ties it to the work as a whole. It is stated clearly, though the claim is somewhat familiar and not very developed.
- Row B: "Amir hides and watches while Hassan is attacked by Assef in the alley after the kite tournament." - Identifies the specific wrong accurately, including the later framing of Hassan. This is precise evidence, but it is mostly plot setup and gets little interpretation beyond linking cowardice to the later repair.
- Row B: "Hosseini makes the violence almost welcome to Amir, as if the pain finally pays for what he allowed before." - Good commentary connecting the beating by Assef to atonement as punishment. It is the strongest analysis in the essay, but it is not tied to a literary technique beyond a general reference to description, and the 'split lip' claim is asserted without much support.
- Row B: "Hassan can never forgive Amir, because Hassan is dead, so the person whose forgiveness matters most is out of reach." - Directly addresses the question of completion and who can declare the debt paid. The point is relevant but stated briefly and not developed into a sustained argument.
- Row B: "This moment echoes the kite tournament of the past, and it suggests that Amir has changed." - Notes the kite motif as a technique, but the commentary is thin and does not explain how the echo shapes meaning. Technique discussion stays limited.
- Row C: "it shows that Sohrab is a real person and not just a way for Amir to feel better." - Begins to raise the tension that atonement can become self-serving, which hints at sophistication. It appears in one sentence and is not carried through the essay, so it does not earn the sophistication point.
- Row C: "Amir is not fully free of his past, yet he is no longer defined only by his failure, and that is the most the novel allows." - A reasonable concluding judgment that acknowledges complexity, but it largely repeats the thesis rather than extending it or placing it in a broader context.

Sample essay (low; scored 3/6: thesis 1, evidence 2, sophistication 0)
In The Kite Runner by Khaled Hosseini, Amir tries to make up for what he did to Hassan. This shows that atonement is important in the novel and it affects the whole story.

Amir's wrong happens when he is a boy in Kabul. After the kite tournament Hassan is attacked by Assef and Amir watches and does not help him. Later Amir is so guilty that he lies and makes it look like Hassan stole from him, so that Hassan and his father Ali leave the house. This is the wrong that Amir carries for the rest of the book.

Because of this, Amir makes many choices. He moves to America with Baba and he grows up and becomes a writer and marries Soraya. But he still feels guilty and he never forgets what he did. When Rahim Khan calls him and says there is a way to be good again, Amir goes back to Afghanistan, which is dangerous because of the Taliban. He finds out that Hassan is dead and that Sohrab is Hassan's son. Amir has to save Sohrab from Assef, who is now a Taliban man. Amir gets beaten up badly by Assef and this is like the punishment he never got when he was young. Then Sohrab uses a slingshot to save him.

In the end Amir takes Sohrab to America and adopts him. Sohrab hardly talks, but at the end Amir runs a kite for him and Sohrab smiles a little. This shows that Amir is somewhat forgiven. The author uses the kite as a symbol of childhood and it comes back at the end to show Amir can start over.

So atonement shapes Amir's life and the novel shows that you can make up for the past by doing good things, even though Hassan is gone.
- Row A: "Amir tries to make up for what he did to Hassan." - This only says the character tries to make up for a mistake, which the rubric says does not earn the thesis point. It takes no position on whether atonement can be completed.
- Row A: "you can make up for the past by doing good things, even though Hassan is gone" - The ending gestures at a position on completion, but it is vague and not set up as a claim defended through the essay. It is too late and too thin to count as a defensible interpretation.
- Row B: "Hassan is attacked by Assef and Amir watches and does not help him." - This correctly identifies the specific wrong and is accurate, but it is plot summary with no commentary on how it shapes the meaning.
- Row B: "Amir gets beaten up badly by Assef and this is like the punishment he never got when he was young." - This is the best moment because it begins to explain what the beating means, but it does not connect to the question of whether the debt is paid or to Hassan's absence.
- Row B: "The author uses the kite as a symbol of childhood and it comes back at the end to show Amir can start over." - This names a symbol but offers little explanation of how it creates meaning. The claim that Amir is forgiven is not examined, for example whether Sohrab's small smile settles the debt.
- Row C: "Amir is somewhat forgiven." - There is no exploration of tension, such as atonement as healing versus self-punishment, or who can declare the debt paid. The argument stays simple and is not sustained.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

lines_of_reasoning: Atonement as self-erasure: the character punishes himself so completely that the penance cuts him off from life, and the work suggests that endless self-punishment is a second wrong. This fits novels about a disgraced officer or soldier who exiles himself.

Atonement that is never finished because the victim is dead: forgiveness is impossible, so the character has to choose between permanent guilt and forgiving herself. This fits stories of wartime betrayal or a child's false accusation.

Atonement through a substitute: the character repays the debt to a stand-in, for example by raising another child or protecting a stranger. The work asks whether such displaced repair actually counts. This fits immigrant family sagas and frontier novels.

Atonement as vanity or control: the penitent's acts of repair serve his image more than the wronged person's needs, and the work exposes this through irony. This fits social novels of class and charity.

Atonement completed through confession and acceptance: the work suggests that repair requires facing the victim directly rather than performing good deeds. This fits novels of reconciliation between siblings or estranged friends.

Atonement passed down through generations: descendants inherit a family's or community's guilt, which raises the question of who is able to finish the payment. This fits multigenerational novels about slavery, colonialism, or land theft.

Atonement as a source of new wrongs: zeal to make things right leads the character to harm others, and the work questions whether moral debt can be calculated at all. This fits tragedies of obsessive justice or revenge disguised as repair.
defensible_positions: The work suggests atonement can never be completed, only lived with, and that accepting this is the real resolution.
The work presents atonement as worthwhile only when it serves the person who was harmed instead of the guilty person's conscience.
The work shows that the pursuit of atonement becomes a new identity, and that this identity is itself a kind of prison.
The work argues that forgiveness, not effort, is what finishes atonement, so the penitent is never in control of it.
common_pitfalls: Retelling the plot of the wrong and the repair without explaining what the pattern means for the work as a whole.
Choosing a work where the character feels guilt but never makes choices driven by atonement, and stretching the work to fit the prompt.
Treating revenge or simple regret as if it were atonement.
Ignoring the question of completion, or simply announcing that the character is redeemed without evidence.
Moralizing about guilt in general instead of analyzing the chosen work.

samples.essay:
In Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner, Amir spends most of his adult life trying to make up for the winter afternoon when he watched Hassan get raped in an alley and did nothing. The novel never lets him pay that debt back, though. Hassan is dead before Amir even tries, so the only person who could forgive him is gone. What Hosseini suggests instead is that atonement can't be finished; it can only be passed forward, and even then it is partial and has its own costs. Amir does not become "good again" by erasing the wrong. He becomes good by agreeing to carry it.

The first choices Amir makes after the alley are not atonement at all, which matters for how we read the later ones. Amir can't stand to be near Hassan, so he pelts him with pomegranates and begs him to hit back. Hassan just crushes one against his own forehead. Amir wants to be punished because punishment would close the account, and Hassan refuses to do it. Then Amir plants his birthday money and watch under Hassan's mattress so Baba will send him away. Hassan takes the blame, Baba forgives him, and Ali and Hassan leave anyway. In this early section, guilt makes Amir do more harm. He doesn't try to fix the wrong; he tries to get rid of the witness. The pomegranate scene shows that the victim's forgiveness (or his refusal to condemn) is not something Amir can force out of him, and this idea comes back at the end of the book.

When Rahim Khan calls Amir to Pakistan and tells him there is a way to be good again, it looks like the novel is promising completion. But Rahim Khan also reveals that Hassan was Baba's son, so Amir's betrayal was of his own brother. This revelation adds something to the story: guilt runs in the family. Baba built an orphanage and gave to everyone, and Rahim Khan explains these deeds as Baba's way of making up for betraying Ali. Baba's charity helped strangers but never told Hassan the truth. Amir realizes his father's goodness and his father's lie were part of the same thing. So the novel sets up a test: will Amir repeat Baba's pattern of public good deeds covering a private wrong, or will he actually deal with the person his family harmed?

He goes after Sohrab, and the scene with Assef is where Hosseini's symbolism is strongest. Amir gets beaten so badly that he laughs, because for the first time he feels he is getting what he deserved. His lip is split in a way that echoes Hassan's harelip, as if the beating marks him with his brother's face. Then Sohrab saves him with a slingshot, the same weapon Hassan once used to hold Assef off when they were children. This mirroring could be read as Amir's redemption being complete, the past finally reenacted and corrected. I think the details actually point the other way. Amir is still the one being saved, and a child is still doing the brave thing for him. The scene repeats the past, it doesn't reverse it.

The aftermath supports this reading. Amir breaks his promise that Sohrab will never go back to an orphanage, and Sohrab tries to kill himself in the hotel bathtub. Amir's effort to repair one wrong produces a new one, almost exactly like his earlier betrayal of Hassan's trust. Even in America Sohrab barely speaks. The ending, where Amir runs a kite for Sohrab in a park and gets a small lopsided smile, is deliberately small. Amir himself says it doesn't fix everything. The kite brings back the tournament where everything went wrong, but now Amir is the one running for someone else.

So Hosseini does not reward Amir with forgiveness, because the only person who could give it is dead. Instead the novel moves the meaning of atonement from paying off a debt to taking on a duty. Baba's kind of redemption, generous to strangers and silent to the person he wronged, is the version the book rejects. Amir's is incomplete and clumsy, but it is aimed at the right person, and the novel suggests that's as close to good again as anyone gets.

annotations.quote: What Hosseini suggests instead is that atonement can't be finished; it can only be passed forward, and even then it is partial and has its own costs.
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that takes a clear position on whether atonement can be completed (it can't) and ties it to the meaning of the whole novel. It also sets up a line of reasoning: the victim is gone, so repair has to be passed forward, and repair has costs.

annotations.quote: He becomes good by agreeing to carry it.
annotations.comment: Makes the thesis sharper by turning the idea of 'being good again' from paying off a debt into carrying a burden, which the closing paragraph comes back to.

annotations.quote: Hassan just crushes one against his own forehead.
annotations.comment: Specific, accurate scene used as evidence. The commentary that follows explains that Amir wants punishment to 'close the account,' which links the scene to the question of completion.

annotations.quote: He doesn't try to fix the wrong; he tries to get rid of the witness.
annotations.comment: Commentary reads the framing of Hassan for theft as guilt that causes new harm, which ties directly to the prompt's idea of a mistake driven by guilt.

annotations.quote: His lip is split in a way that echoes Hassan's harelip
annotations.comment: Analyzes symbolism and mirroring (the split lip, the slingshot) as literary techniques, so the essay covers more than one technique and how each contributes to meaning, as Row B's top score requires.

annotations.quote: Amir's effort to repair one wrong produces a new one
annotations.comment: Follows a later choice driven by repair (the broken orphanage promise) and explains how it makes the repair itself a new harm. The commentary stays tied to the line of reasoning.

annotations.quote: This revelation adds something to the story: guilt runs in the family.
annotations.comment: Begins a sustained point about inherited guilt. The Baba/Amir comparison runs through the rest of the essay, which gives it a wider context.

annotations.quote: This mirroring could be read as Amir's redemption being complete, the past finally reenacted and corrected. I think the details actually point the other way.
annotations.comment: Takes on an alternative reading and answers it with evidence from the text, so the complexity isn't oversimplified.

annotations.quote: Baba's kind of redemption, generous to strangers and silent to the person he wronged, is the version the book rejects.
annotations.comment: Brings the Baba comparison to a conclusion about which kind of atonement the novel approves of. This shows the sophistication is developed across the essay, not stated in a single sentence.

samples.essay:
In The Kite Runner, Amir lives for most of his life under the weight of what he did to Hassan, and Hosseini uses his long effort to make up for it to suggest that atonement can never be fully completed, only continued. Amir's attempt to repay the wrong gives his adult life direction, but the novel shows that the person he wronged is gone, so the debt can only be paid in a different form than he first imagined.

The wrong is specific. As a boy in Kabul, Amir hides and watches while Hassan is attacked by Assef in the alley after the kite tournament. Hassan had been loyal to Amir, and Amir did nothing. Afterward Amir makes it worse by driving Hassan and his father Ali out of the house, framing Hassan as a thief. Because Amir's guilt comes from cowardice and betrayal, the repair he later attempts has to be about courage and loyalty.

Amir's later choices are shaped by this. In America he becomes a writer and marries Soraya, but his success feels hollow, because the secret is still there under his life. When Rahim Khan calls him back to Pakistan and says there is a way to be good again, Amir goes, even though it is dangerous. In Afghanistan he learns that Hassan was his half-brother and that Hassan has been killed, leaving a son, Sohrab. Amir's decision to rescue Sohrab from Assef, who now serves the Taliban, is the clearest act of atonement. This time he does not hide. He takes a beating from Assef, and Hosseini makes the violence almost welcome to Amir, as if the pain finally pays for what he allowed before. The split lip he gets is described as a kind of healing, which shows that Amir sees atonement partly as punishment.

However, the novel does not let the repair feel finished. Hassan can never forgive Amir, because Hassan is dead, so the person whose forgiveness matters most is out of reach. Sohrab is also not a simple payment. After the rescue he is traumatized, and when he is threatened with being sent back to an orphanage, he attempts suicide. Amir's good deed does not erase the damage, and it shows that Sohrab is a real person and not just a way for Amir to feel better.

The ending is hopeful but modest. Sohrab barely speaks, and then he gives a small smile when Amir flies a kite for him and offers to run it for him. This moment echoes the kite tournament of the past, and it suggests that Amir has changed. But it is only a smile, not a cure. By making the ending small, Hosseini argues that atonement is not a debt that is paid once but a way of living, a lifelong responsibility to do right by the next generation. Amir is not fully free of his past, yet he is no longer defined only by his failure, and that is the most the novel allows.

annotations.quote: Hosseini uses his long effort to make up for it to suggest that atonement can never be fully completed, only continued
annotations.comment: Defensible thesis that takes a position on whether atonement can be completed and ties it to the work as a whole. It is stated clearly, though the claim is somewhat familiar and not very developed.

annotations.quote: Amir hides and watches while Hassan is attacked by Assef in the alley after the kite tournament.
annotations.comment: Identifies the specific wrong accurately, including the later framing of Hassan. This is precise evidence, but it is mostly plot setup and gets little interpretation beyond linking cowardice to the later repair.

annotations.quote: Hosseini makes the violence almost welcome to Amir, as if the pain finally pays for what he allowed before.
annotations.comment: Good commentary connecting the beating by Assef to atonement as punishment. It is the strongest analysis in the essay, but it is not tied to a literary technique beyond a general reference to description, and the 'split lip' claim is asserted without much support.

annotations.quote: Hassan can never forgive Amir, because Hassan is dead, so the person whose forgiveness matters most is out of reach.
annotations.comment: Directly addresses the question of completion and who can declare the debt paid. The point is relevant but stated briefly and not developed into a sustained argument.

annotations.quote: This moment echoes the kite tournament of the past, and it suggests that Amir has changed.
annotations.comment: Notes the kite motif as a technique, but the commentary is thin and does not explain how the echo shapes meaning. Technique discussion stays limited.

annotations.quote: it shows that Sohrab is a real person and not just a way for Amir to feel better.
annotations.comment: Begins to raise the tension that atonement can become self-serving, which hints at sophistication. It appears in one sentence and is not carried through the essay, so it does not earn the sophistication point.

annotations.quote: Amir is not fully free of his past, yet he is no longer defined only by his failure, and that is the most the novel allows.
annotations.comment: A reasonable concluding judgment that acknowledges complexity, but it largely repeats the thesis rather than extending it or placing it in a broader context.

samples.essay:
In The Kite Runner by Khaled Hosseini, Amir tries to make up for what he did to Hassan. This shows that atonement is important in the novel and it affects the whole story.

Amir's wrong happens when he is a boy in Kabul. After the kite tournament Hassan is attacked by Assef and Amir watches and does not help him. Later Amir is so guilty that he lies and makes it look like Hassan stole from him, so that Hassan and his father Ali leave the house. This is the wrong that Amir carries for the rest of the book.

Because of this, Amir makes many choices. He moves to America with Baba and he grows up and becomes a writer and marries Soraya. But he still feels guilty and he never forgets what he did. When Rahim Khan calls him and says there is a way to be good again, Amir goes back to Afghanistan, which is dangerous because of the Taliban. He finds out that Hassan is dead and that Sohrab is Hassan's son. Amir has to save Sohrab from Assef, who is now a Taliban man. Amir gets beaten up badly by Assef and this is like the punishment he never got when he was young. Then Sohrab uses a slingshot to save him.

In the end Amir takes Sohrab to America and adopts him. Sohrab hardly talks, but at the end Amir runs a kite for him and Sohrab smiles a little. This shows that Amir is somewhat forgiven. The author uses the kite as a symbol of childhood and it comes back at the end to show Amir can start over.

So atonement shapes Amir's life and the novel shows that you can make up for the past by doing good things, even though Hassan is gone.

annotations.quote: Amir tries to make up for what he did to Hassan.
annotations.comment: This only says the character tries to make up for a mistake, which the rubric says does not earn the thesis point. It takes no position on whether atonement can be completed.

annotations.quote: you can make up for the past by doing good things, even though Hassan is gone
annotations.comment: The ending gestures at a position on completion, but it is vague and not set up as a claim defended through the essay. It is too late and too thin to count as a defensible interpretation.

annotations.quote: Hassan is attacked by Assef and Amir watches and does not help him.
annotations.comment: This correctly identifies the specific wrong and is accurate, but it is plot summary with no commentary on how it shapes the meaning.

annotations.quote: Amir gets beaten up badly by Assef and this is like the punishment he never got when he was young.
annotations.comment: This is the best moment because it begins to explain what the beating means, but it does not connect to the question of whether the debt is paid or to Hassan's absence.

annotations.quote: The author uses the kite as a symbol of childhood and it comes back at the end to show Amir can start over.
annotations.comment: This names a symbol but offers little explanation of how it creates meaning. The claim that Amir is forgiven is not examined, for example whether Sohrab's small smile settles the debt.

annotations.quote: Amir is somewhat forgiven.
annotations.comment: There is no exploration of tension, such as atonement as healing versus self-punishment, or who can declare the debt paid. The argument stays simple and is not sustained.

blueprint.concept: atonement as a force that shapes later choices
blueprint.central_idea: Trying to make up for a wrong can give a life direction and can also take that life over. Fiction often leaves it unclear whether the debt can ever be cleared, or who has the authority to declare it cleared.
blueprint.complexity: Atonement is both a way out of guilt and a trap. It can heal, but it can also turn into self-punishment, vanity, or avoidance of the person who was harmed. Whether it can be finished depends on forgiveness, on whether the victim is still alive, and on whether the self can ever accept that it has paid.
